planting.note: Plant grafted or seedling stock in fall or early spring into deep, well-drained loam; this is the primary wild progenitor of the cultivated apple, native to the Tian Shan mountain forests of Kazakhstan and surrounding Central Asia, and is grown mainly by collectors, breeders, and genebanks rather than for orchard fruit production.

directions: This is the wild species from which nearly all cultivated apple varieties ultimately descend, discovered growing in extensive seed-grown forests on the slopes of the Tian Shan range. Seedling populations show enormous variation in fruit size, color, and flavor, ranging from tiny and astringent to large and sweet, which is why breeders and genebanks collect and maintain diverse accessions rather than a single named form. Grow it on deep, well-drained soil with cold winters and warm summers similar to its Central Asian mountain habitat, and expect considerable disease susceptibility variation between individual seedlings since wild populations have not been selected for orchard pest and disease resistance. It is primarily of interest for breeding programs seeking genetic diversity, disease resistance genes, and climate adaptability rather than for direct fruit production.
sources: Forsline et al., Wild Apples of Central Asia

planting.note: Plant hardwood cuttings in spring into well-drained, calcareous or rocky soil; winter grape is native to the limestone hills of Central Texas and northern Mexico and is grown almost exclusively by breeders and rootstock producers for its tolerance of high-lime soils, not for its fruit.

directions: Winter grape is a vigorous, high-climbing vine native to the limestone escarpments of the Edwards Plateau and Rio Grande region, prized by rootstock breeders for its unusual tolerance of calcareous, high-pH soils that induce lime-chlorosis in most other grape species. It is one of the key parent species behind widely used rootstocks such as SO4, 5BB, and 161-49C, which combine its lime tolerance with the phylloxera resistance of other American species. Grow it on dry, rocky, alkaline sites in full sun where it will scramble over fences or into trees; the small, dark, tart berries ripen late and are of minor interest except to wildlife. This species is best suited to collectors maintaining rootstock breeding germplasm rather than home fruit growers.
sources: Galet, Grape Varieties and Rootstock Varieties

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in fall or early spring into average, well-drained soil; this extremely cold-hardy wild species from Siberia and northern China is used by breeders mainly as a source of hardiness and as rootstock/seedling understock rather than for its small, tart fruit.

directions: Siberian crabapple is one of the hardiest apple relatives in cultivation, tolerating winter lows far beyond what domestic apples can withstand, which has made it a foundational parent in cold-climate ornamental and fruiting crabapple breeding programs. Trees bear a profusion of small white flowers in spring followed by abundant pea-sized red or yellow fruit that persists on the branches well into winter, valuable for birds and for rootstock seed production. Plant in full sun on any well-drained soil; it tolerates extreme cold, wind, and poor sites better than most Malus species. Because seedlings come fairly true from seed, it has long been used as an inexpensive, uniform seedling rootstock in regions too cold for standard apple rootstocks.

planting.note: Plant grafted or seedling trees in fall or early spring into well-drained, even poor or dry soil; snow pear is a wild Central and Southeastern European species valued by perry makers and breeders for its bitter, tannic fruit and its distinctive silvery foliage.

directions: Snow pear is a wild European species named for the dense white-woolly down covering its young leaves and shoots, giving the whole tree a striking silvery-gray cast through spring and summer. It is a direct ancestor of many traditional English and French perry pears, which inherited its high tannin and acid content, qualities undesirable in dessert pears but essential for a well-structured fermented perry. Grow it in full sun on lean, dry, even calcareous soils where it tolerates drought and poor fertility better than most pears. The hard, gritty, astringent fruit is inedible fresh but becomes palatable after bletting or pressing, and the tree is also planted ornamentally for its felted foliage and tolerance of difficult sites.

planting.note: Plant hardwood cuttings in spring into moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Amur grape is a wild East Asian species native to the Russian Far East, Manchuria, and Korea, grown chiefly by cold-climate breeders and collectors for its extreme winter hardiness.

directions: Amur grape is among the most cold-hardy grape species known, surviving winter temperatures that would kill most Vitis vinifera and even many American hybrids, which has made it a key parent species in Russian, Chinese, and upper-Midwest cold-climate breeding programs. The broad, often deeply lobed leaves turn vivid red to purple in autumn, giving the vine strong ornamental value beyond its fruiting use. Grow it in fertile, moisture-retentive soil in full sun with a sturdy trellis, as vines are vigorous climbers in the wild forests of its native range. Fruit clusters are small with dark, thin-skinned, tart berries that are mostly used in breeding for hardiness and disease resistance rather than grown for direct fresh eating or winemaking.

planting.note: Plant grafted or seed-grown trees in spring into humid, well-drained forest-margin soil; this rare wild citrus from the Garo Hills of Meghalaya in northeast India and adjacent Bhutan is maintained mainly in germplasm collections and by citrus collectors, not grown as a conventional fruit crop.

directions: Indian wild orange, also called the Garo hill lemon, is one of the most primitive and taxonomically significant species in the citrus group, considered by many researchers to be close to the ancestral stock from which cultivated citrus diverged. It grows naturally as an understory tree in subtropical forest in a very limited range and is now critically endangered in the wild, making cultivated specimens important for ex-situ conservation. Grow it in humid, partially shaded conditions with rich, well-drained soil that mimics a forest-margin habitat, protecting it from hard frost and prolonged drought. The small, sour, seedy fruit is of little culinary value, and the species is grown almost exclusively by citrus researchers, botanical gardens, and dedicated collectors interested in citrus evolution and genetic diversity rather than for fruit production.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in fall or early spring into average, well-drained soil; tea crabapple is a wild Chinese species valued by orchardists as a seedling apple rootstock and by gardeners for its disease-resistant ornamental display.

directions: Tea crabapple is a wild Chinese species notable for its apomictic seed, meaning seedlings grow nearly identical to the parent tree without cross-pollination, a trait that made it a widely used uniform seedling rootstock for grafted apples before clonal rootstocks became standard. In spring it produces an abundance of fragrant pink-fading-to-white flowers followed by small yellow-green to red fruit that persists into fall, and in parts of China the young leaves are dried and brewed as a folk tea, giving the species its common name. Grow it in full sun on any well-drained soil; it is notably resistant to fire blight and several other apple diseases compared to domestic cultivars. Its strong disease resistance and uniform seedling habit continue to make it valuable to breeders and rootstock producers as well as to collectors of ornamental flowering crabapples.
